sections.h2: Your options for a fast Tucson sale
sections.html:
Start by choosing a listing with an agent, a for-sale-by-owner effort or an as-is cash purchase. Whichever you pick, the closing in Pima County ends the same way: escrow at a title company, a deed recorded by the Pima County Recorder and a sales affidavit attached to the deed.

A regular listing works for a well-kept house when you can wait on a buyer's mortgage. Cash makes more sense if repairs were put off, a tenant lives there, probate is pending or a tax bill needs clearing fast. Whatever the route, plan for the inspection: buyers here test the roof, the cooling system and the drainage. Tucson covers a large desert basin, and a house can have little in common with one a few miles away.

Pull together these papers first:

  • Payoff letters from lenders, plus the Assessor parcel number
  • Permit paperwork for casitas, room additions, pool work or replaced HVAC and water heaters
  • Utility status, since a house with power or gas off for months needs a reconnect permit
  • Your current Pima County Treasurer tax statement

Tucson has 548,371 residents, up from 542,629 at the 2020 census. Owners live in 51.8% of homes. Median home value is $266,200, median rent is $1,145, and the median household earns $57,073 across 228,020 households.

Those are citywide figures. A midtown house near the University of Arizona and a foothills property can sit far apart on price, so compare recent sales on your own street.

After monsoon rain, buyers' inspectors look at roof flashing, stucco cracks, window seals and drainage around the foundation. The monsoon season officially starts June 15, and storms can last into September. The Santa Cruz River is dry much of the year but floods in heavy seasonal rain, so ask the city whether your parcel falls in a floodplain or wash zone before you set a price. Paving and grading in washes, hillside zones and floodplains always needs a permit.

sections.h2: Permits that come up in a Tucson sale
sections.html:
Most residential work in Tucson needs a permit and inspection. The Planning and Development Services Department (PDSD) runs the process through the Tucson Development Center Online portal. PDSD is in the Public Works Building at 201 N. Stone Avenue, and the phone is 520-791-5550.

The owner is responsible for plans and a permit for:

  • New or replacement water heaters, furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners, with load and sizing calculations for HVAC
  • Electrical service increases and panel replacement or repair
  • Detached accessory structures over 200 square feet, such as storage sheds
  • Porches, additions, garages and remodels of existing structures
  • Walls and fences, which need a zoning site plan review, and a building permit with engineered design above 7 feet

Review time depends on the project. The Express Lane handles same-day items such as residential electrical and plumbing work. Fences and pools go to the Fast Lane with a 15-day target, and alterations and new buildings go to the Standard Lane with a 30-day goal. Interior finishes such as paint, carpet and cabinets need no permit, and neither does a like-for-like toilet swap.

You can still get a permit for finished work, though the same requirements apply. Submit a full set of construction drawings and complete the inspections. The owner should stop any ongoing work until the permit exists.

A vacant house raises a second issue. A permit is required to reconnect electric or gas service if the utility has been off to a residential structure for 6 consecutive months. The permit costs $135.59 and covers an inspection for obvious code or life-safety problems. Property in a Historic Preservation Zone, Neighborhood Preservation Zone or designated Historic Landmark needs a permit for any development, plus a design review.

Casitas are allowed, one per residential lot, if they meet size and height standards. Rental units count as commercial property for permit purposes. Homeowners may use the owner-builder exemption under A.R.S. 32-1121 for their own residence, but it does not apply to any project that requires a building permit or where materials and labor exceed $1,000. Permit approval does not override HOA covenants on the property.

If a permit turns out to be missing, tell the buyer early. Many cash buyers will take the house as it stands and adjust their price, which can be faster than finishing inspections yourself, but get that agreement in writing and keep any drawings or receipts you have for the work.

sections.h2: Pima County property tax due dates
sections.html:
Tucson house taxes go to the Pima County Treasurer, who sends the bill. Anything over $100 splits into two payments.

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after 5 p.m.
First halfOctober 1November 1
Second halfMarch 1May 1

The tax year 2026 second-half postmark deadline is May 3, 2027. Interest on the first installment is waived if you pay the whole year before 5 p.m. on December 31. Call the Treasurer at 520-724-8341.

Have the title company order a payoff so any unpaid tax is taken from your proceeds when you close. If you want to contest your value, petition the Pima County Assessor within 60 days of the postmark on a Notice of Value mailed on or before March 1. Disputes concern value, and the tax itself stays payable while you wait.

Documents that transfer real property go to the Pima County Recorder with a complete legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value under A.R.S. 11-1133. A deed submitted without a complete affidavit is rejected and returned.

An exempt transfer must be accompanied by the Arizona Department of Revenue exemption letter and number. Formatting rules apply too: an original signature, print of at least ten point, a page no bigger than 8.5 by 14 inches and a 2-inch top margin on page one. Photo identification is required from anyone who brings documents in person. Staff cannot offer legal advice, so lean on your title company or attorney.

In a typical sale, the title company orders payoffs and searches the record, you and the buyer sign, funds are released, and the deed goes to the Recorder. Take a photo ID to the signing table, along with your lender payoff letter and any lease if tenants live there.

faqs.q: How long can a sale take in Tucson?
faqs.a: The route and the state of the title decide it. Once title work is clear, a cash buyer can close when you say, but a buyer with a mortgage adds appraisal and loan time. Ask your title company what it needs for a Pima County payoff and recording.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace my water heater or air conditioner in Tucson?
faqs.a: Yes. Tucson requires a permit and inspection for new or replacement water heaters, furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners. HVAC permits need load and sizing calculations.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Tucson house that has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: You can sell it, but disclose the work and ideally permit it first. Tucson allows permits for work already done if you supply full drawings and pass inspections. Ask PDSD at 520-791-5550 what applies to your address.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax on a Tucson house?
faqs.a: Collection belongs to the Pima County Treasurer, while the Pima County Assessor sets values. November 1 and May 1 are the dates after which each half is late.

faqs.q: What is required to record a deed in Pima County?
faqs.a: The deed needs a full legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value. An exempt transfer instead carries the Department of Revenue exemption letter and number, and anyone filing in person shows photo identification.
